solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One in mob clash turning chaotic

indicators.note: something put in another thing ends up sitting inside it
turning things over and around changes their order, so the letters get rearranged

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lone figure caught up in a crowd brawl that is spiralling out of control.
explanation.walkthrough: Put I among the letters of MOB CLASH, then rearrange all nine to get SHAMBOLIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Shambolic is informal British usage for something disorganised and messy, which is a close synonym of chaotic.

clue.text: Second’s words manage to inspire fighter

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so the answer is drawn inside the surrounding text

blocks.note: letters running from the end of the first word into the start of the third

explanation.surface: A boxer's second gives an encouraging pep talk to rouse the fighter in the corner.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxing second and his pep talk are a smokescreen: the answer sits in plain sight, from secondS through WORDS to MANage.
explanation.definitionFit: A swordsman is someone who fights with a blade, so he is one particular kind of fighter.

indicators.note: without its conclusion a word has lost its final letter

blocks.note: to judge something is to weigh it up or evaluate it

explanation.surface: A magistrate who never reaches a verdict is made to look foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: ASSESS with its last S dropped leaves ASSES.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling people asses is an old insult meaning they are stupid, so the word is a plain synonym for fools.

clue.text: Bra seems almost undone being dirty

indicators.note: almost all of something means it falls just short, missing its last letter
something undone has been taken apart, so the letters are free to be put back in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the word with its final S removed

explanation.surface: A half-unfastened bra suggests something rather racy is going on.
explanation.walkthrough: SEEMS loses its last letter to give SEEM; BRA plus SEEM, rearranged, gives BESMEAR. 'Dirty' here is a verb, not the adjective the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To besmear is to smear all over or soil, so it works as the verb to dirty something.

indicators.note: an embrace wraps arms around someone, so one part is placed around another

blocks.note: a leaning is an inclination or tendency
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A political commentator analyses a drift towards right-wing views.
explanation.walkthrough: LEANING wraps around R to give LEARNING. The political capital on Right is just the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Learning is the acquiring of knowledge through reading and lessons, the same activity as study as a noun.

clue.text: Turn over motor, even losing volume

indicators.note: losing something means it is taken away and no longer there

blocks.note: a motor is informal British for a car
taken as written
V is the abbreviation for volume; this is the letter removed

explanation.surface: Advice on turning over a car engine smoothly while turning the volume down.
explanation.walkthrough: CAR followed by EVEN with its V taken out gives CAREEN. 'Turn over' suggests starting an engine but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To careen a ship is to tip it over on its side for cleaning, and more broadly to tilt or overturn.

clue.text: Foliage from meadow beginning to fall

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: lea is a poetic word for a meadow
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: In autumn leaves start coming down across a meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: LEA is a crossword favourite for a meadow; add F to make LEAF.
explanation.definitionFit: Foliage is the collective word for the green growth on plants, and a single leaf is one unit of it.

clue.text: Plant seeds while missing hard ground

indicators.note: something missing has gone, so a letter is removed
ground up means crushed into bits, so the letters are reformed in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
the word with its H taken out
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils; this is the letter removed

explanation.surface: A gardener sows seeds while the hard soil goes undug.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove H from WHILE, then rearrange SEEDS plus WILE to get EDELWEISS. 'Ground' reads as soil but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Edelweiss is a small white-flowered alpine species, so it is one example of a plant.

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so one part goes within another

blocks.note: a feed is informal for a big meal
T is the abbreviation for tons

explanation.surface: A guest of honour is toasted at a banquet with mountains of food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With meal' reads as one idea, but 'with' only joins, and the meal is a noun: a feed, as in having a good feed.
explanation.definitionFit: To fete someone is to honour them publicly with festivities, so feted means much praised or celebrated.

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising something lifts it so it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information or details
someone blushing goes red

explanation.surface: Someone goes red-faced while a frank talk about sex goes into the specifics.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN is British slang for information; RED written upwards gives DER, making GENDER.
explanation.definitionFit: Gender and sex are both used for the category of male or female, so they are near synonyms.

clue.text: Hops finally put into grain kilns

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter is used
putting something into another thing places it inside

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
oats are a cereal grain

explanation.surface: Brewing talk: hops added to grain, then everything dried in kilns.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter goes in the middle of the grain, not at its end. Oast houses are the kilns used in Kent to dry hops, so the surface fits nicely.
explanation.definitionFit: An oast is a kiln for drying hops, a distinctive building in the English countryside.

indicators.note: something placed in another thing sits within it

blocks.note: taken as written
hands are workers, as in farmhands or deckhands
to welcome someone is to greet them

explanation.surface: Handshakes all round as a warmly received business deal is struck.
explanation.walkthrough: Hands here means workers, as in farmhands, not the palms of a handshake.
explanation.definitionFit: A deal is an arrangement two parties accept, which is exactly what an agreement is.

clue.text: Make out Queen name on record

blocks.note: a record is a vinyl disc
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual abbreviation for the Queen
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Trying to read the band name Queen printed on an old album.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across answer, 'on record' puts the other pieces after the record. Queen is the monarch, Elizabeth Regina, not the rock band.
explanation.definitionFit: To make out something faint is to perceive or detect it, the same as discerning it.

indicators.note: after says one piece is placed behind another, so the clue's order is swapped

blocks.note: a termination is an end
money that is due is owed

explanation.surface: A sacked worker gets the pay still owed after being let go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Money due' looks like one phrase, but money belongs with Provided as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To endow a college or prize is to give it a permanent fund, so endowed means supplied with funds.

indicators.note: following means coming behind, so the clue's order is swapped

blocks.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway, with the 1 read as the letter I
a dash is a short sprint

explanation.surface: A literal account of a mad rush along the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the London to Leeds motorway, and its 1 is read as I. 'Literal' is printers' jargon for a typo, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: In printing and publishing a literal is a typographical error, a wrong letter set in type.

indicators.note: something done unusually is not in its normal order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rare sighting: an American congressman unexpectedly secured something.
explanation.walkthrough: The nine letters of GOT RARE US rearrange to SURROGATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A surrogate is a person standing in or acting for another, which makes them a deputy or representative.

clue.text: Rapid attacks in daring swoops, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives up its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letters of these five words

explanation.surface: A military report on lightning strikes carried out by bold swooping aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: the opening letters of five words spell RAIDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Raids are sudden surprise assaults, quick strikes into enemy territory, matching rapid daring attacks.

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the end is cut off

blocks.note: safe as in certain or sure; its last letter goes
prised open, as a lid is forced with a lever

explanation.surface: Someone is shocked to find their safe has almost been broken open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Safe' is not the strongbox but the adjective, as in a safe bet, meaning certain.
explanation.definitionFit: To be stunned is to be astonished or taken aback, the state of being caught unawares.

indicators.note: around means encircling, so one part surrounds another

blocks.note: BO is body odour, plus the S of the possessive
feeling rotten is feeling rough, ill

explanation.surface: A foul smell hangs over decaying neighbourhoods.
explanation.walkthrough: BO is body odour. Rotten boroughs were notorious near-empty constituencies in old Britain, which the surface echoes.
explanation.definitionFit: A borough is a town or district with its own local council, so boroughs are administrative areas.

indicators.note: occasionally means every so often, so only every other letter counts

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

explanation.surface: Your nose now and then catches a whiff of something foul nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: Take every other letter of NEAR REEKS, starting with the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Nares is the anatomical Latin term for the openings of the nose, a medical synonym for nostrils.

indicators.note: something housed in a place is kept inside it

blocks.note: a modest person is shy
a worker ant is the standard crossword worker

explanation.surface: A poorly paid labourer lives in a humble hut.
explanation.walkthrough: The worker in crosswords is very often an insect, the worker ant.
explanation.definitionFit: A shanty is a crude makeshift dwelling, the same kind of ramshackle hut as a shack.

blocks.note: surface reading: a sportsman who puts points on the board for his teammates
setter's reading: someone who writes musical scores for others to perform

explanation.walkthrough: The sporting sense of scoring for teammates misleads; a score is written music and the players are musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who writes music produces scores that orchestral musicians then perform, so the description fits.

indicators.note: carrying something means holding it within, so one part sits inside another

blocks.note: a page is a young servant
OTT, over the top, means extravagant

explanation.surface: A waiter brings out an extravagant platter.
explanation.walkthrough: PAGE holds OTT to give POTTAGE. OTT is short for over the top.
explanation.definitionFit: Pottage is a thick soup or stew, a type of cooked dish best known from Esau's mess of pottage.

clue.text: Child is quiet, quietly biting lip

indicators.note: biting means having teeth around something, so one part closes on another

blocks.note: SH is the call for quiet
a lip is the rim of a jug or cup
P, piano, is the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: A shy youngster stays silent, nervously chewing their lip.
explanation.walkthrough: Quiet and quietly are two different pieces: the hush call, then the musical direction piano.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrimp is an affectionate informal name for a small person, especially a little kid.

blocks.note: first meaning: resolve or appetite for something
second meaning: to tolerate, as in being unable to stand it

explanation.surface: Taking a firm stance requires resolve.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a principled stand, but the two words are separate senses of one word, noun and verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the stomach for something means the resolve to face it, and to stomach something is to put up with it.

clue.text: Part of ropes is always fibre

indicators.note: part of a phrase is a piece of it, so the letters lie inside the following words

blocks.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: A sailor explains that rope is always made of some fibre.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from the end of ropeS through IS to the start of ALways.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is the stiff strand from an agave plant, widely used to make twine, so it is a fibre.

indicators.note: a vacated place has been emptied, so only the outside letters are left

blocks.note: to worst someone is to beat them
the word emptied of its middle

explanation.surface: A dreadful landlord takes his holiday out in the open air.
explanation.walkthrough: Worst is a verb meaning defeat, OUTDO; OWNER emptied leaves OR. 'Worst' looks like a superlative adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfresco is borrowed from Italian, meaning in the open air, so it describes something done outdoor.

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
china is Cockney rhyming slang, china plate meaning mate, so chinas are pals

explanation.surface: An antique porcelain piece is decorated with precious stones.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, 'topped with' puts O above PALS. China is Cockney rhyming slang: china plate rhymes with mate.
explanation.definitionFit: Opals are iridescent precious stones, so they are one kind of gemstone.

indicators.note: an embrace wraps around someone, so one part is put inside another

blocks.note: beginning and starting mean the same
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A scandal as someone starts cosying up to the political left.
explanation.walkthrough: STARTING takes in L to give STARTLING; this mirrors 4 Down, which embraced Right.
explanation.definitionFit: Something startling causes a sudden jolt of surprise or alarm, so it is shocking.

clue.text: Horses like circling westerly watering hole

indicators.note: heading west in an across answer means going right to left
to circle something is to go all the way round it

blocks.note: as and like are synonyms
a watering hole is slang for a bar

explanation.surface: Horses wander round a desert watering hole in a cowboy western.
explanation.walkthrough: The watering hole is a pub, not a pond, and westerly means written backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Arabs are a famous breed of fine, spirited horse, so the plural names horses of that breed.

indicators.note: covering something means going over and around it

blocks.note: a lid is a cover
the heart of sweet is its middle letter, a standard crossword trick

explanation.surface: A made-up cover story hides a secret lover.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweetheart is not a lover here but the heart of sweet, its middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabricated here means made up a falsehood, the past tense verb for telling an untruth.

indicators.note: oddly means taking the odd-numbered positions, first, third and fifth

blocks.note: a posse is a gang, plus the S of the possessive
the odd-numbered letters

explanation.surface: The Crazy Gang, a British comedy troupe, were strangely calm.
explanation.walkthrough: The Crazy Gang were a famous British comedy group, but Crazy is the definition. POSSE'S plus SED from steady.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone possessed behaves wildly as if controlled by a demon, so it means frenzied or mad.
